what_it_does: Cameras in self-driving cars, robots, and AR headsets capture every frame at full resolution — say 4K — even though most of the image (sky, empty road, blank walls) contains almost no useful information. IRIS teaches the image signal processor (the specialized chip that converts raw camera data into usable images) to recognize which parts of a frame matter, then compress the unimportant parts before even storing the frame, so that downstream vision software processes a smaller, cheaper image without losing accuracy.
method_in_detail:
The idea. A camera-based vision pipeline has two parts: a frontend (the image signal processor, or ISP, which turns raw sensor data into a clean image) and a backend (the CPU or GPU that runs object detection, localization, or classification). Currently the ISP hands a full-resolution image to the backend every frame. But the ISP already computes two useful intermediate results — an edge sharpness map (used to enhance image details) and motion vectors (used to reduce noise by comparing with the previous frame) — and then throws them away. IRIS reuses these 'free' byproducts to decide which image regions are worth keeping at full resolution.

How it works. The ISP divides the image into a grid of small 16x16 pixel blocks. For each block it computes an IRIS Saliency Score (ISS) — a simple formula combining how many edges are in the block (edge density, from the sharpness processing already running) and how fast that block is moving (motion magnitude, from the motion estimation already running). A block where cars or pedestrians are visible has many edges and often high motion; sky has neither.

Blocks are then grouped into larger 32x32 or 64x64 regions. If the maximum saliency score in a group falls below a threshold set by the application, the whole group is downsampled to 16x16 (shrinking it 4× or 16×) before being written to the framebuffer (main memory). A small Region Resolution Map is saved alongside the image so the backend knows what resolution each block is in.

The key design choice. All three new units — the Saliency Scorer, the Quad grouping unit, and the Downsampling unit — run in parallel with existing ISP stages using data those stages already produce, so they add zero latency to the ISP pipeline. The circuit-level design is validated as cycle-accurate hardware description code.

Backend impact. For vision transformer image classification, mixed-resolution input naturally reduces the number of tokens to process. For the ORB-SLAM3 visual localization algorithm, IRIS adds an iterative feature extraction pass: regions are processed in order of descending saliency score and extraction stops when new features yield diminishing returns.

The result. For localization, IRIS cuts average latency by 22.8%, tail latency by 10.5%, and energy by 22.5%. For image classification (using a DeiT-S Vision Transformer), it cuts average latency by 37.5% and energy by 41.5%, with less than 1% accuracy drop. The new hardware adds only 0.027 mm² of chip area.
